questiontext.text: For a string S, what does the Z-value Z[i] measure?

answer.text: The length of the longest substring starting at position i that is also a prefix of S

feedback.text: Correct — Z[i] matches S against itself starting at i.

answer.text: The length of the longest suffix of S ending at position i

feedback.text: No — Z-values compare against the prefix, not a suffix.

answer.text: The number of times character S[i] appears in S

feedback.text: No — Z has nothing to do with character frequency.

answer.text: The index of the next occurrence of S[i]

feedback.text: No — Z[i] is a length, not an index.

generalfeedback.text: Z[i] is the length of the longest common prefix of S and the suffix of S starting at position i.

questiontext.text: Using the Z-algorithm for pattern matching (n = text length, m = pattern length), what is the total time complexity?

feedback.text: Correct — the Z-array is computed in a single linear pass.
No — no logarithmic factor is involved.
That is naive matching; the Z-algorithm avoids re-scanning.
No — the algorithm is linear, not quadratic.

generalfeedback.text: The Z-box amortizes work so each position is charged O(1), giving O(n + m) over the concatenation.

questiontext.text: To find all occurrences of pattern P in text T with the Z-algorithm, on what string do you compute the Z-array?

answer.text: P + separator + T, where the separator is a character not in the alphabet

feedback.text: Correct — the separator stops Z-values from exceeding m.
No — without a separator Z-values could bleed across the boundary.
No — reversal is not part of the Z-algorithm.

answer.text: P alone; T is never needed

feedback.text: No — you must scan T to find matches.

generalfeedback.text: On P$T, any position i (inside the T region) with Z[i] = m marks an occurrence of P in T.

questiontext.text: Which statements about the Z-algorithm are true? (select all that apply)

answer.text: It runs in linear O(n + m) time

feedback.text: Yes — a single amortized pass builds the Z-array.

answer.text: It is a single-pattern exact matching method

feedback.text: Yes — like KMP, it searches for one pattern at a time.

answer.text: It requires O(n * m) time in the worst case

feedback.text: No — it is linear, not quadratic.

answer.text: It natively searches many patterns simultaneously like Aho-Corasick

feedback.text: No — that is Aho-Corasick's role, not the Z-algorithm's.

generalfeedback.text: The Z-algorithm is a simple linear single-pattern method; multi-pattern search is Aho-Corasick's domain.

questiontext.text: What auxiliary space does the Z-algorithm use to store its Z-array over the concatenation (n = text length, m = pattern length)?

feedback.text: Correct — one Z-value is stored per position of the P$T string.
No — the Z-array itself grows with the input length.
No — the space is linear, not quadratic.
No — you store a value for every position, so it is linear.

generalfeedback.text: The Z-array holds one entry per character of P + separator + T, giving O(n + m) space.

questiontext.text: On the string P + separator + T, a position i where Z[i] equals m (the pattern length) indicates an occurrence of the pattern.

feedback.text: Correct — a full-length prefix match means P appears there.
Z[i] = m means the m-length prefix (the pattern) matches at i.

questiontext.text: The Z-algorithm and KMP solve the same single-pattern matching problem in linear time, using different formulations.

feedback.text: Correct — both are O(n + m) single-pattern methods with different internal structures.
They are indeed two linear-time formulations of the same task.

questiontext.text: The array computed by this algorithm, whose entry at index i is the longest prefix-match length starting at i, is called the ______ array.

feedback.text: Correct.
Correct.
